title: Gait Abnormality - Chronic Subdural Haematoma
patient_instructions: You are Arthur Nguyen, a 76-year-old retired man who has been having difficulty walking for the past 2-3 months and are worried you are 'having a stroke'. If asked to clarify what you mean by difficulty walking, it is WEAKNESS of the whole LEFT leg (not pain, not dizziness) - and you have also noticed your LEFT arm feels weaker than the right. It has come on gradually and slowly got worse. If asked about injuries: about 3 months ago you had a FALL at home and hit your head; you did not think much of it at the time, no vomiting, brief or no loss of consciousness. Important: you take APIXABAN (a blood thinner) for atrial fibrillation. You have mild headaches and feel a bit light-headed at times. No slurred speech, no visual problems, no numbness, no loss of consciousness now, no fits. No back pain, no bladder or bowel problems, no saddle numbness. No tremor. No neck pain. You live with your wife. Your IDEAS: you fear a stroke. Your CONCERNS: becoming disabled. Your EXPECTATIONS: to find out what is wrong and get it treated. Affect: cooperative, a little anxious, answers clearly.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice / emergency department. Arthur Nguyen, 76, presents with 2-3 months of difficulty walking and is worried about a stroke. Tasks: (1) Take a focused history over approximately 6 minutes, clarifying what he means by difficulty walking and working through a grouped neurological/MSK differential. (2) Explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials, and address his stroke concern. You do not need to examine the patient. The examiner is looking for a clarified complaint, a grouped differential, elicitation of the head-injury and anticoagulation history, and recognition that this is a neurosurgical emergency requiring immediate imaging.
examiner_instructions: The candidate should first clarify 'difficulty walking' (pain vs weakness vs balance) - here it is subacute left arm and leg weakness. Reward a grouped differential (UMN/brain, LMN, muscle, cerebellar, vestibular, MSK/antalgic, falls contributors). Critically, the candidate must probe for a fall/head injury (3 months ago) and anticoagulant use (apixaban), and recognise that an elderly, anticoagulated patient with a subacute focal deficit after head trauma has a chronic subdural haematoma until proven otherwise - a neurosurgical emergency. Expected plan: immediate same-visit non-contrast CT head, check coagulation, withhold apixaban and discuss reversal (andexanet alfa or prothrombin complex concentrate) and neurosurgical referral; investigation must NOT be deferred. Note: polymyalgia rheumatica causes proximal pain/stiffness, NOT true weakness - do not reward it as a weakness cause. Address the stroke concern honestly. Screen cauda equina/cord compression red flags. Use the rubric.

criteria: Clarifies what 'difficulty walking' means (pain vs weakness vs balance)
Elicits fall/head-injury history and anticoagulant (apixaban) use
Screens cord-compression/cauda equina and falls-risk factors
Identifies chronic subdural haematoma with reasons (subacute focal deficit + head injury + anticoagulation)
Gives grouped differentials and addresses the stroke concern with reasons it is less likely
Recognises neurosurgical emergency - immediate non-contrast CT head, no deferral
Checks coagulation, withholds apixaban, discusses reversal and neurosurgical referral
Explains diagnosis in plain language and addresses stroke fear; explores ICE

red_flags: New focal neurological deficit in an elderly anticoagulated patient after head injury - chronic subdural haematoma, neurosurgical emergency
Headache with early-morning vomiting, worsening deficit or reduced GCS - raised intracranial pressure
Bladder/bowel disturbance or saddle anaesthesia - cord compression / cauda equina requiring urgent MRI
Acute FAST-positive features (face/arm/speech) - acute stroke pathway
australian_guidelines: Anticoagulation reversal: in a confirmed acute intracranial bleed on apixaban, withhold the drug, check coagulation, and consider reversal (andexanet alfa or prothrombin complex concentrate) per haematology - do not defer imaging or investigation

Stroke Foundation / RACGP falls guidance: structured falls assessment with lying and standing blood pressure, medication review (sedatives, antihypertensives, anticoagulants) and vision/hearing screen
eTG neurology: an elderly anticoagulated patient with a focal deficit after head trauma requires immediate non-contrast CT head and neurosurgical referral
learning_objectives: Clarify a vague 'difficulty walking' complaint into a localisable deficit
Construct a grouped neurological/MSK differential for gait disturbance
Recognise chronic subdural haematoma in the anticoagulated elderly after head injury
Initiate emergency imaging and anticoagulant reversal appropriately
key_points: Chronic subdural haematoma evolves over weeks-months and commonly presents as walking difficulty
Head injury + anticoagulation + subacute focal deficit is the diagnostic triad
Polymyalgia rheumatica causes proximal stiffness/pain, not true weakness or a raised CK
Do not defer imaging - this is a same-visit neurosurgical emergency

citations.claim: Weakness with an upper- vs lower-motor-neuron pattern is investigated with CT/MRI head for a central lesion and EMG/nerve conduction studies for neuromuscular causes.
citations.source: Churchills Pocketbook of Differential Diagnosis, p.529

citations.claim: A vague presentation such as walking difficulty should be approached with a safe, systematic diagnostic strategy.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition, p.229

citations.claim: Movement and neuromuscular disorders form part of the gait differential.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition, p.3578
